input:
This cost review looks at a cross-dock transfer operation and sets out what it currently costs to run on an annual basis. The transfer involves 609 km per trip, and the carrier charges $1.71 per km, with a total of 575 trips being undertaken per year. When these figures are combined, the annual transport cost comes to $599k, which represents a significant line item in the logistics budget.

The figures presented here are drawn from carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so they reflect what was actually paid over that period rather than any estimate or projection. It is important to note that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the cost per kilometre is effectively spread across both loaded and unloaded legs of the operation. This is a meaningful consideration, because it means the headline cost reflects the full operational reality of the transfer, including the return journeys that generate no revenue.

Understanding the structure of this cost is an important first step in any broader review of the transfer operation, since the annual figure is built up from a small number of clear components: the distance travelled on each trip, the rate charged per kilometre, and the total number of trips made across the year. Any change in one of these components would flow directly through to the annual total.

It is also worth bearing in mind that each of these components can move independently of the others, so that the annual figure may change from one year to the next for quite different reasons, whether because the carrier revises its rates, because the route itself changes, or because the volume of goods passing through the dock rises or falls.
target:
A cross-dock transfer costs $599k per year. The figure is built from three components: 609 km per trip, a carrier rate of $1.71 per km, and 575 trips per year.

The costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months, not estimates. They are therefore a record of what the transfer cost at the trip rate and trip count of that period, and they will move with either quantity: the annual figure is the product of the three components, so a change in trip distance, in the per-kilometre rate, or in trip frequency changes the total in direct proportion. Empty running is included in the trip count. The rate is consequently spread over loaded and empty kilometres alike, and the cost of a loaded kilometre is higher than the rate suggests when the return leg runs empty. Any comparison of this transfer against an alternative routing or carrier must be made on the same basis, with empty running inside the trip count on both sides, or the comparison will understate the cost of whichever operation hides its empty legs. The review establishes the cost of the transfer as it is currently run; it does not price any alternative.

The three components also show where any future change in the cost will come from. The rate per kilometre is a carrier price and changes at renegotiation. The trip count follows the volume of goods moving through the dock and changes with the business itself. A review that reports only the annual total cannot distinguish a cost increase caused by a higher carrier rate from one caused by more trips, and the two call for different responses: the first is a purchasing question, the second a capacity question. The invoice base makes the distinction recoverable, because each invoice carries its own distance and its own rate.
